posts.caption: The farrier showed up at 7:15 with his coffee and his good mood, which is how I knew the invoice would hurt. He spent forty minutes under Big Red, who held her foot up like she was giving a speech and he was the audience. He trimmed, he rasped, he told her she was doing great. She accepted this as her due. Then he handed me a slip of paper with a number on it, and I read it standing in the barn aisle in my slippers. I did what any reasonable person would do. I went to the feed room and looked at the grain bins for a while.
posts.first: I keep the farrier's invoices in a folder labeled Misc, which is the only honest label I've found. Last month's is on top. I've taken it out and read it twice, as if it might change. It hasn't. The horse got new feet and I got a very long afternoon of thinking.

posts.caption: The hay guy delivers on the second Tuesday of the month, and he has been backing that truck up to my barn door for six years without being thanked by anyone with hands. This month he got out, looked at the stack, looked at me, and said the bales looked a little crooked. They did. They were crooked in a way that suggested a very small supervisor. We restacked all hundred and forty in the cold, and I paid him in coffee and the good cookies. He took the cookies and left the coffee. He knows things.
posts.first: I write the delivery dates on the barn wall in marker, because my phone calendar and I stopped speaking in March. The second Tuesday is circled in red. Pudding has never read it. He's somehow always at the door by seven.

posts.quote: I spent the weekend stacking hay, chipping ice, and apologizing to a gate. My sister asked if I'd rested. I said yes.
posts.first: I told her about the frozen trough and the gate that only opens inward when my hands are full. She laughed in the right places. Then I hung up, put on my boots, and went back out to check the water, because it was nine and the barn lights were still on.

posts.caption: The spigot outside the feed room froze solid on Wednesday, so I've been carrying kettles of hot water down the aisle in my husband's old coat. It takes four trips. I measured. The mash needs to be exactly the temperature of a good cup of tea, which I check with my wrist like a mother testing a baby bottle. Last night I got it wrong and Homebody stared at me over the bucket for a full minute without a single bite. I added more water, and she sighed like I'd finally learned. Eleven years, and I'm still being trained.
posts.first: My mother used to warm my pajamas on the radiator before bed, and I never thought about it until I was standing in a freezing barn with a kettle. Now I understand. Some things you only learn by being the one who carries the water.

posts.caption: I loaded at 5:40 a.m., braided in the dark, and drove ninety minutes to a lot full of trailers I didn't recognize. The sign at the gate said Dog Agility. I sat in the truck for a while with the heater on. The Diva, to her credit, stepped off the trailer like she'd been invited, took one look at forty terriers, and walked a slow lap of honor. Somebody clapped. I bought a coffee and a donut and we drove home. The show was the following weekend. She has not let me forget it.
posts.first: I keep that fly bonnet in the tack room in a bag with her name on it. It's lavender, with little crocheted ear tips. She has worn it exactly four times, and every time she has acted as though it was her idea. The terriers got ribbons. She got more attention.

posts.caption: The yearling arrived in September, all legs and opinions, and attached herself to the Old Timer the way a new employee attaches herself to the one coworker who isn't panicking. He tolerates it. He stands at the corner of the paddock where the sun hits first, and she stands about six feet off, trying to look casual. Every evening I find them in the same spot, chewing in the same rhythm, not saying a word. I brought out my coffee last Sunday and sat on the fence to watch. Nobody told me to leave, so I stayed until the coffee was cold.
posts.first: My dad used to say you can learn everything about a barn by watching its oldest horse. I've watched the Old Timer for nine years now. Mostly he teaches me when to sit down. I'm still working on it.
